scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that the partner
network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) feels very slow -- they are sure the inter-AS peering
between router1 and router2 is congested and adding huge latency. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text: A complete four-phase investigation found no network fault anywhere in the simple_bgp topology. Phase 1 reachability showed 0% packet loss and a round-trip time of approximately 1.25 ms in both directions between pc1 (195.11.14.2) and pc2 (200.1.1.2) — well within normal virtual-lab baseline. Phase A infrastructure sweep found no ACL or firewall drop rules, no static ARP poisoning, no IP or gateway misconfiguration, and no duplicate MAC addresses on any of the four devices. Phase B confirmed the BGP control plane is fully healthy: both router1 (ASN 1) and router2 (ASN 2) have all FRR daemons active (watchfrr, zebra, bgpd), a single BGP session in the Established state, and their respective prefixes (195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24) correctly advertised. The tc_snapshot found no traffic-control shaping on any of the six inspected interfaces — all show only the Linux default fq_codel qdisc, which is a latency-reducing discipline, not a bandwidth limiter or delay injector. Phase D pressure_sweep found no stress or flood tool running on any device and no CPU or socket pressure. The user's claim that inter-AS peering is "congested and adding huge latency" is directly contradicted by live measurements: there is no tbf rate-limiter, no netem delay, no resource overload, and no routing anomaly. The perceived slowness is not attributable to any network fault present in the topology at the time of investigation.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly reports 0% packet loss and ~1.25 ms stable RTT between pc1 and pc2 over an Established eBGP session, confirming the baseline is healthy (no congestion).

The agent's claims are directly backed by the logged tool outputs (reachability, infra/l2 sweep, BGP and tc snapshots, pressure sweep). The inference that there is no network-caused latency is logical from those observations; the only minor gap is that reachability used a small sample (tx=2) rather than a long sustained ping, but multiple independent checks nevertheless support a healthy baseline.
